definition: In language modeling, Katz back-off is a generative n-gram model that estimates the conditional probability of a word given its history in the n-gram.
details: It accomplishes this estimation by backing off through progressively shorter history models under certain conditions. By doing so, the model with the most reliable information about a given history is used to provide the better results. The model was introduced in 1987 by Slava M. Katz. Prior to that, n-gram language models were constructed by training individual models for different n-gram orders using maximum likelihood estimation and then interpolating them together.

explainer.lead: Katz back-off is a generative n-gram language model that estimates a word's probability from its history, falling back to shorter histories when longer ones lack reliable data. It replaced earlier practice of training separate n-gram models and interpolating them.

tiers.eli5: If you have no good data on what usually follows a long phrase, you look at a shorter part of it instead; you trust the most detailed look you can, and shorten the look only when the detail is missing.
tiers.practitioner: Used as a classic baseline and smooth-ing technique in statistical language modelling; the pitfall is that back-off weights and discounting must be tuned, and the model still suffers from sparsity at high n-gram orders.
tiers.paperLevel: Estimates the conditional probability of a word given its n-gram history by backing off to progressively shorter histories under certain conditions; introduced by Slava M. Katz in 1987.

explainer.example: For the history 'the cat sat on the', if the 5-gram was not observed in training, the model backs off to the 4-gram or 3-gram counts to assign a probability.
